Female Madeira rockfish reach reproductive maturity at a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], a size typically attained within their second year of life in coastal waters. Field surveys indicate that this length threshold is closely tied to the onset of vitellogenesis and marks the transition from the immature juvenile stage to the reproductively viable adult phase. At this size, individuals have completed the majority of their somatic growth, though they continue to increase in length until reaching an ultimate total length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], which appears to represent the asymptotic size for most populations based on extensive mark-recapture data from the Mediterranean basin. However, some particularly large specimens collected from deeper, cooler habitats along the Atlantic coast of Morocco have been documented at an ultimate total length of 17.8 centimeters [Li = 17.8 centimeters], suggesting moderate geographic variation in maximum attainable size that may be correlated with local productivity regimes or thermal conditions. This species exhibits a typical scorpionfish body plan, with a robust, laterally compressed torso and an elaborate array of spines and cirri that provide effective camouflage among rocky substrates.

Hatching of the fertilised eggs occurs after an embryonic period of approximately eleven days [ab = approximately eleven days] when water temperatures are held constant at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a developmental timeline consistent with that reported for other temperate scorpaenids. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], placing them among the smallest larval stages documented for this genus. This minimal mass at the onset of the exotrophic transition imposes a tight energetic constraint on the larvae, which must locate suitable zooplankton prey within a few days of yolk absorption completion or face starvation. The prolarvae drift passively within the plankton for several weeks, during which time they undergo gradual morphological transformation, including the differentiation of the pectoral fins and the initial ossification of the cranial skeleton. Field collections of ichthyoplankton suggest that larval abundance peaks during the late summer months, coinciding with elevated temperatures and heightened primary productivity in nearshore environments.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], individual Madeira rockfish have been observed to live for a maximum of 13 years [am = 13 years], although wild specimens are rarely recorded beyond approximately a decade, likely due to elevated predation pressure on benthic juveniles and sub-adults. This lifespan, while modest compared to some deep-water scorpaenids, is considerable for a relatively small-bodied coastal species and reflects a life-history strategy characterized by slow growth and delayed reproduction. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to the larger of the two asymptotic lengths has been estimated from morphometric relationships, yielding a value of 134.5 grams [Wwi = 134.5 grams] when calculated using a volumetric conversion based on an assumed spherical egg diameter of 1.5 millimeters, a proxy often employed for energetic scaling analyses. Mature adults therefore range considerably in mass, with smaller individuals around 14 centimeters attaining a projected ultimate wet weight of 64.3 grams [Wwi = 64.3 grams], based on local length-weight regressions specific to this species. These size-mass relationships are routinely used by fisheries biologists to infer biomass from visual census transects.

Reproduction in this species is characterized by a moderate output, with females producing up to approximately 22 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 22 eggs per day] during the peak spawning season when maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This daily fecundity accumulates over an extended reproductive period, such that total annual fecundity can be substantial. Gravid individuals are most frequently encountered between late spring and early autumn, during which time they may release multiple batches of pelagic eggs into the water column. The eggs are small, buoyant, and lack any adhesive structures, facilitating wide dispersal by prevailing currents. Fertilisation is external, occurring shortly after gamete release during spawning events that often involve several males pursuing a single female. The resulting planktonic eggs are transparent and measure approximately 1.5 millimeters in diameter, containing a single oil globule that aids in buoyancy regulation throughout the incubation period. Egg survival is presumed to be highly variable and strongly dependent on local hydrographic conditions.

The overall life history of Madeira rockfish reflects a balance between modest reproductive output and extended parental investment in the form of large, yolk-rich eggs that support a relatively long embryonic period. Juveniles settling into benthic habitats recruit to rocky reef environments at sizes substantially below the minimum length at puberty for females of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], and they spend their first year primarily as cryptic inhabitants of crevices and overhangs. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Scorpaena porcus reveal broadly similar patterns in age at maturity and maximum size, though the Madeira rockfish maintains a slightly higher asymptotic mass relative to body length. Physiological studies examining oxygen consumption in this species have noted that metabolic rates scale predictably with body mass, with smaller individuals exhibiting elevated mass-specific oxygen demand. Future work should focus on quantifying the energetic trade-offs between growth and reproduction across the species' geographic range, particularly at the warmer margins of its distribution where thermal stress may limit foraging activity and reduce lifetime fecundity.
